title: Canadian tax records show how tightening changes the distribution of income growth
summary: Yaz Terajima and Carolyn Wilkins find that Canadian households’ market incomes respond unevenly to monetary policy. A tightening shock persistently reduces income growth more at the top of the distribution than near the bottom. On the authors’ estimates, this offsets some of the tendency for income growth to become more concentrated in the upper tail during expansions. The result concerns the distribution of pre-tax market income, which includes earnings, business income and investment returns. It does not measure a change in households’ consumption, wealth or after-tax disposable resources. The paper’s combination of tax records and independently identified policy shocks matters for interpreting that distinction (sections 2–6).

The household panel is constructed from Canadian administrative records covering 1982–2019. The underlying longitudinal database draws a 20% sample of individual tax filers, with family information used to follow households through time. The primary sample restricts the household head to ages 18–65 and applies income thresholds described in section 2. The long span helps the authors distinguish responses to policy shocks across multiple cycles. It also brings narrower coverage for certain components: limited partnership income, for example, is reported separately only from 1988. Appendix A describes the source data, while the detailed component tables in appendix F make these coverage differences visible.

The authors first ask how gains and losses in market income are distributed when the economy expands and contracts. Their central measure compares the spread between the 90th percentile and the median income-growth rate with the spread between the median and the 10th percentile. That asymmetry, known as Kelley skewness, moves more consistently with the business cycle than the overall variance does. Lower- and higher-income households drive much of the cyclical movement. Among income sources, investment income, especially capital gains, plays an important part. Where a household sits in the distribution of income levels is distinct from where its annual gain or loss falls in the distribution of growth rates (sections 2–3).

The policy exercise estimates household responses to an unexpected one-percentage-point tightening over horizons of up to five years. Section 5 and figure 12 compare groups by their pre-existing income levels. In year one, the top decile experiences a decline in market-income growth 0.741 percentage points larger than the fifth decile. The estimate for the lowest decile in that year cannot be distinguished statistically from the middle group’s. Differences persist across later horizons. Labour earnings account for much of the differential response, with business and investment income also contributing. Thus the income source most important for cyclical asymmetry need not be the largest contributor to the difference in policy effects across deciles.

Section 6 tests the aggregate implication separately. A one-percentage-point tightening reduces the estimated skewness measure by 1.878 percentage points in year one, statistically significant at the 5% level. The two underlying percentile spreads are individually imprecise, and year one is the only horizon with a significant skewness response in figure 13. The aggregate exercise has 32–36 annual observations, depending on horizon, far fewer than the millions of household records behind the panel estimates. Taken together, the results support the authors’ interpretation that monetary policy can dampen a particular source of cyclical market-income inequality. They supply neither a household welfare ranking nor an argument that a rate increase would raise low-income households’ incomes in absolute terms.

questions.question: Does the distributional response survive alternative measures of an unexpected tightening?
questions.detail: The results depend on annualizing and extending the shock series and separating unexpected policy from changing economic conditions. Repeat the estimates with alternative identification methods on overlapping years and compare the household and aggregate responses at the same horizon. This matters particularly for the skewness estimate, where the effective number of independent annual observations is small relative to the size of the tax panel.

questions.question: How closely do changes in market-income growth translate into changes in disposable resources?
questions.detail: Wages, realized gains and business income enter the tax-record measure differently across the income distribution. Taxes, transfers, debt payments and portfolio values can alter households’ ability to spend following a rate shock. Compare market-income estimates with disposable income and cash flow for the same deciles. The distinction is important for translating a distributional result into a view about household demand.

questions.question: Would the same pattern appear across different labour and asset-market conditions?
questions.detail: Capital gains account for much of the cyclical asymmetry, while labour income drives an important part of the tightening response. Examine periods with similar changes in output but different asset-price movements and wage growth. Report uncertainty by income source and horizon and test the sensitivity to the sample restrictions. This would help assess when the historical Canadian estimates are most informative.
